key_decisions.decision: Uses the earlier established God Almighty for El Shaddai, retaining Luz rather than substituting Bethel; uncertainty of the divine title belongs in apparatus.
Preserves the adoption claim, its temporal boundary, and the significant Ephraim-first order with explicit comparison to Jacob’s first sons.
Keeps subsequent children distinct from the two adopted sons and explains the name reckoning specifically within inheritance.
Carries the personal force of died upon me, retains the indefinite distance and Paddan form, and does not invent a causal link between Rachel’s burial and the adoption.
Retains the strong inability-to-see statement alongside verse 8 and names the one bringing the sons to prevent pronoun confusion. Israel is named again as the one embracing them.
Makes the likely owner of the knees explicit without portraying the sons as infants or claiming a particular adoption ritual as certain.
Makes the crossing visible and retains the deliberate younger/firstborn contrast; the verb’s skillful/deliberate sense is noted.
Preserves blessing Joseph through his sons, the ancestral walk, and the shepherd image; begins poetic lineation without losing the continuous syntax.
Retains angel beside the parallel divine descriptions without resolving its identity doctrinally; preserves redeem, names, and multiplication rather than adding fish to the main text.
Retains doubled knowing, both positive statements about Manasseh, and the stronger younger-son promise without mapping nations to a later political scheme.
Clarifies the blessing formula’s function, preserves the embedded wish and reversed names, and keeps the narrator’s explanation separate from quoted poetry.
Makes the Hebrew plural you audible so the return promise is not restricted to Joseph alone.
Preserves the extra portion and Jacob’s first-person claim to armed acquisition; notes Shechem wordplay and does not rewrite it to harmonize with chapters 33–34.
